allowed_dependency_manifest.content: Let n, k, l ∈ Z with 0 ≤ k, l ≤ n. Define R(q) = [n choose k]_q / [n choose l]_q in the natural rational-function setting for Gaussian q-binomial coefficients. If R(q) lies in a polynomial ring in q (i.e., R(q) has only finitely many nonnegative powers of q with coefficients in the relevant coefficient ring), then when written as R(q) = Σ_i c_i q^i, every coefficient c_i satisfies c_i ≥ 0.

forbidden_claims.statement_nl: Let [n choose k]_q denote the Gaussian q-binomial coefficient. Prove that for all integers n, k, l with 0 ≤ k, l ≤ n, if [n choose k]_q / [n choose l]_q is a polynomial in q, then that polynomial has only nonnegative coefficients.

forbidden_claims.statement_nl: For integers A, B, d with A >= B >= 0 and d >= 0, define Q_{A,B,d}(q) := prod_{i=1}^d (1 - q^(A+i)) / (1 - q^(B+i)), with the empty product equal to 1 when d = 0. Assume Q_{A,B,d}(q) belongs to Q[q]. Let S be the weighted polynomial ring Q[x_1, ..., x_d] graded by deg(x_i) = B+i; when d = 0 interpret S as Q. Then there exist homogeneous polynomials f_1, ..., f_d in S such that deg(f_i) = A+i for every i, and for each i the image of f_i in S/(f_1, ..., f_{i-1}) is not a zero-divisor. Equivalently, Q_{A,B,d}(q) is realized by a homogeneous regular sequence in a weighted polynomial ring with variable weights B+1, ..., B+d and relation degrees A+1, ..., A+d.

payload.statement_nl: Let k be a field, let d be a nonnegative integer, let w_1,...,w_d be positive integers, and let S = k[x_1,...,x_d] with weighted grading deg(x_i)=w_i. Let I be a homogeneous ideal of S. If, over an algebraic closure of k, the common zero locus of I in affine d-space is exactly the origin, then S/I is finite-dimensional as a k-vector space.

external_facts_used: Hilbert's Nullstellensatz over algebraically closed fields

result_payload.proof_nl:
First suppose d = 0. Then S = k. The only ideals of S are 0 and S; their zero loci in affine 0-space over an algebraic closure are respectively the unique point and the empty set. Since the zero locus is assumed to be exactly the origin, we must have I = 0. Hence S/I = k, which is finite-dimensional.

Now assume d >= 1. Let kbar be an algebraic closure of k, set T = kbar[x_1,...,x_d], and let J be the ideal of T generated by I. Because J is generated by I, it has the same common zero set in kbar^d as I; by hypothesis this zero set is just the origin. By Hilbert's Nullstellensatz, any polynomial in T that vanishes on V(J) lies in sqrt(J), equivalently some power of it lies in J. Each coordinate function x_i vanishes at the origin, hence on V(J), so for each i there exists N_i >= 1 with x_i^(N_i) in J.

Claim: J intersect S = I. One inclusion is clear: every element of I lies in J and also in S. For the reverse inclusion, take f in J intersect S. Then f = sum_{nu=1}^r u_nu g_nu for some g_nu in I and u_nu in T. Let W be the k-subspace of kbar spanned by 1 and by all coefficients of the finitely many polynomials u_nu. Choose a k-basis 1 = e_1, e_2, ..., e_m of W. Each u_nu can be written uniquely as u_nu = sum_{j=1}^m e_j h_{nu,j} with h_{nu,j} in S. Therefore
f = sum_{j=1}^m e_j F_j, where F_j := sum_{nu=1}^r h_{nu,j} g_nu is in I.
If sum_{j=1}^m e_j P_j = 0 with P_j in S, then comparing the coefficient of each monomial shows that all P_j = 0, because the e_j are k-linearly independent. Thus such an expression is unique for polynomials in T whose coefficients lie in W. Since f itself lies in S, its coefficients lie in k and therefore in W, and we also have f = e_1 f + sum_{j=2}^m e_j 0. By uniqueness, F_1 = f and F_j = 0 for j >= 2. In particular f lies in I. So J intersect S = I.

Applying the claim to x_i^(N_i) in J intersect S, we get x_i^(N_i) in I for every i.

Now any monomial x_1^(a_1)...x_d^(a_d) with some a_i >= N_i lies in I, since it is divisible by x_i^(N_i). Hence the residue classes of the finitely many monomials x_1^(a_1)...x_d^(a_d) with 0 <= a_i < N_i for all i span S/I over k. Therefore S/I is finite-dimensional as a k-vector space.
result_payload.proof_summary: Extend I to the polynomial ring over an algebraic closure. Nullstellensatz shows that each coordinate x_i has some power in the extended ideal, because the only common zero is the origin. An explicit coefficient-comparison argument proves that the extended ideal contracts back to I, so those same powers already lie in I. Hence only finitely many bounded-exponent monomials survive modulo I, and they span S/I.

used_external_facts: Hilbert's Nullstellensatz over algebraically closed fields
